specAnchors.text: describe how thermal energy transfer may take place by conduction, convection and radiation
explain the role of convection in everyday phenomena
explain how emission and absorption of radiation are related to surface and temperature

primer.text: Heating moves energy three ways: through solids by colliding particles (conduction, turbocharged in metals by delocalised electrons), through fluids by density-driven currents (convection), and through nothing at all by infrared waves (radiation). The surface and the state of matter decide which route wins.

modules.title: Conduction, conductors and insulators
sourceHeadings: Example of a conductor and an insulator
modules.opening: Conduction is the main route by which heating moves energy through solids. Metals conduct superbly; non-metals, liquids and gases barely conduct at all — and the poor conductors earn a name of their own, insulators, which is exactly what you want under your feet on a cold bathroom floor.
keyPoints: Conduction moves heating energy through solids by particle jostling.
Metals are extremely good thermal conductors.
Non-metals conduct poorly, and liquids and gases barely conduct at all.
Poor conductors are called insulators, and they prevent energy transfer by conduction.
Materials containing pockets of trapped air are especially good insulators because air is a gas and cannot form convection currents when trapped.

low.restatement: Solids conduct by particle collisions; metals do it best, gases barely at all, and trapped air is the reason fluffy materials insulate so well.
low.analogy: A queue passing buckets hand to hand: a tight queue (solid) passes fast, a scattered crowd (gas) barely passes at all.
low.examPointer: Name the mechanism in answers: heated particles vibrate harder and knock into neighbours, handing energy along.

medium.restatement: The conductor-insulator split is a spectrum: metals at the top, non-metal solids far below, liquids lower still and gases lowest — which is why materials that trap air are the designers’ favourite insulators.
medium.analogy: Rumour spreading in an office (tight desks, fast) versus a city park (people far apart, slow): closeness sets the transfer rate.
medium.examPointer: Trapped-air answers need BOTH halves: air is a poor conductor AND it is trapped so it cannot move to form a convection current.

modules.title: How conduction works, and why metals win
modules.opening: Heat one end of a solid and its atoms vibrate harder, jostling their neighbours and passing energy along atom by atom. Metals add a second delivery service: their delocalised electrons roam freely and collide with atoms, carrying the vibrations — and the heat — far faster than the lattice alone could.
keyPoints: Heating makes a substance’s atoms vibrate harder and knock into their neighbours.
Each collision passes energy from atom to atom through the material.
Metals contain delocalised electrons that can move through the lattice.
The delocalised electrons collide with atoms and help transfer the vibrations through the metal.
This extra transfer mechanism is why metals conduct heat better than non-metals.

low.restatement: Two mechanisms: the lattice passes vibrations by collision, and in metals the free electrons ferry energy between atoms, which is the metals’ winning edge.
low.analogy: Passing a message down a line of people by shoulder taps, while in a metal some runners also sprint along the queue carrying copies.
low.examPointer: The phrase that scores: delocalised electrons collide with atoms, transferring the vibrations through the material faster.

medium.restatement: Particle picture: heating raises the vibration amplitude of lattice atoms; collisions propagate it; electron collisions add a fast parallel channel unique to metals.
medium.analogy: A crowded standing wave at a concert: the push of neighbour on neighbour spreads the sway, and the stewards moving through the crowd spread it faster still.
medium.examPointer: Do not say electrons carry heat like a fluid — say they collide with atoms and transfer energy, which is the model’s actual claim.

modules.title: Convection and convection currents
modules.opening: Fluids — liquids and gases — carry heat by moving themselves: convection. Warm fluid expands, becomes less dense than its surroundings, and rises; cooler fluid sinks into its place; the cycle draws a convection current. Solids are excluded — nothing flows — which is why the mechanism belongs to fluids alone.
keyPoints: Convection moves thermal energy through fluids — liquids and gases — by bulk flow of the fluid itself.
Convection cannot occur in solids.
When a fluid is heated, its particles push apart and the fluid expands.
The hot fluid is less dense than its surroundings, so it rises.
Cooler fluid moves in to take its place; the hot fluid cools, contracts and sinks, forming a convection current.

low.restatement: Heat a fluid, it expands and floats upward; cool fluid replaces it and the loop repeats — a convection current that shuttles energy through the fluid bulk.
low.analogy: A warm-air balloon: heated air lifts the basket because expansion made it lighter per cubic metre than the air around it.
low.examPointer: Convection answers need the density chain: heated → expands → less dense → rises; and the replacement step: cooler fluid sinks in to take its place.

medium.restatement: The current is a closed loop driven by density differences: rise above the heat source, lose energy to the surroundings at the top, contract, sink, and return to be heated again.
medium.analogy: An escalator pair in a shopping centre: one side carries warm air up, the other returns the cooled flow down, and the loop never stops while the heater works.
medium.examPointer: Everyday phenomena to quote: sea breezes, radiators warming a room, boiling water’s rolling motion.

modules.title: Thermal radiation and the mug of coffee
sourceHeadings: Conduction, convection and radiation in a mug of coffee
modules.opening: Every object, whatever its temperature, emits infrared radiation — no particles, no medium, just waves. Hotter objects radiate more per second, and the surface decides how well: black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers, shiny surfaces the worst. A cooling mug of coffee runs all three transfer routes at once.
keyPoints: All bodies emit infrared radiation, whatever their temperature.
A hotter object radiates more infrared in a given time.
Black objects are the best emitters and absorbers of thermal radiation; shiny objects are the worst.
Shiny surfaces reflect radiation, which is why they absorb so poorly.
A hot mug of coffee loses energy by radiation from its surfaces, by conduction through the mug walls, and by convection of the warm air above it.

low.restatement: Radiation is the no-medium route: every object emits infrared, hotter means more, and the surface’s colour and finish set the emit-absorb score, black best and shiny worst.
low.analogy: A spotlight that every object shines all the time, turned up by temperature; the surface is the lampshade, black glass letting everything through, polished metal bouncing it back.
low.examPointer: The mug-of-coffee question wants all three routes named with their surfaces: radiation from the surface, conduction through the walls, convection above the drink.

medium.restatement: Emission and absorption are two sides of the same surface quality: good absorbers are good emitters (black, dull), poor absorbers are poor emitters (white, shiny — shiny reflects instead).
medium.analogy: A good listener is usually a good talker: surfaces that take radiation in easily also give it out easily; the mirror-finish ones do neither.
medium.examPointer: Sort the four surfaces in order when asked: black > dull/dark > white > shiny, for BOTH absorbing and emitting.

glossary.definition: Energy transfer by heating through particle collisions, the main route in solids.
A poor conductor that does not transfer energy by heating well; trapped-air materials are the classic case.
Free electrons in metals that collide with atoms and speed up thermal conduction.
The closed loop of a heated fluid: hot fluid rises, cools, contracts and sinks back.
Infrared emission that every object gives out, needing no medium; black surfaces emit and absorb best.
